staffing_team.text: Any future implementation should include a formal review of applicable NMFS/NOAA confidentiality, cybersecurity, data-management, and records requirements and should establish appropriate controls for transmission, storage, access, and retention. The implementation plan should also evaluate the respective technical and security implications of continuous Starlink transmission versus 4G/Wi-Fi store-and-forward transfer. Q5. Program objective: Is the purpose limited to testing EM on three vessels, or is the contractor expected to design the future operational Hawai'i shortline EM program, including system standards, coverage, review, staffing, costs, and scaling? A: The purpose of the effort includes both pilot EM deployments and support for planning a potential future operational EM program. The Contractor shall procure, install, and evaluate EM systems on three pilot vessels and three trips, assess camera configurations and operational impacts, evaluate data retrieval and transfer procedures, conduct data review and QA/QC, and refine VMPs and review methodologies based on pilot findings. This is designed to inform PWS Section 6.5 that specifically requires the Contractor to support NMFS planning associated with future implementation of an operational EM program. This

oth pilot EM deployments and support for planning a potential future operational EM program. The Contractor shall procure, install, and evaluate EM systems on three pilot vessels and three trips, assess camera configurations and operational impacts, evaluate data retrieval and transfer procedures, conduct data review and QA/QC, and refine VMPs and review methodologies based on pilot findings. This is designed to inform PWS Section 6.5 that specifically requires the Contractor to support NMFS planning associated with future implementation of an operational EM program. This includes developing implementation recommendations; assessing staffing and resource requirements, long-term review requirements, operational costs and logistical considerations; providing recommendations regarding implementation schedules and scaling approaches across the entire fishery; and supporting Government planning discussions and technical meetings. The Final Report shall assess the feasibility of implementing EM in the fishery. Accordingly, the effort is not limited to testing EM on three vessels. The Contractor is expected to use the pilot results to support NMFS's evaluation and planning for potential future operational implementation. The test risk score should be based on an analysis of RNA markers and should not incorporate PSA levels in its algorithm, nor require the DRE (digital rectal exam) prior to collection of the urine specimen. replace existing rat housing equipment that has exceeded 20 years of continuous service and has surpassed its useful operational life. Background DVR supports critical biomedical research programs requiring reliable, high-capacity rat housing systems. The existing legacy rat IVC rack system has exceeded 20 years in service, well beyond the manufacturer-rated and industry-standard service life for IVC equipment of 15 years. This extended service life has resulted in: Increased frequency and cost of maintenance and repairs. Reduced system reliability and an elevated risk of unplanned ventilation, filtration, or containment failure. Diminished availability of OEM replacement parts and discontinued vendor support for legacy components. Outdated, latch-dependent cage-top design that increases staff repetitive-motion and strain injury risk relative to current industry’s best practice. Inconsistent environmental control (airflow distribution, pressure differential) relative to current-generation IVC performance standards. Because the legacy system directly supports active rat colonies used in ongoing biomedical research, its continued degradation constitutes a mission-critical risk: any unplanned failure could result in loss of animals, interruption of active protocols, and noncompliance with anim

d demonstrated to maintain a protective pressure differential and life support in the event of a power failure. Air inlet and outlet valves located at the top of the cage, away from animal level, protected by silicone O-rings, to prevent direct air draft on the animals and reduce the risk of stress and heat loss; non-invasive rack supply and exhaust nozzles external to the cage to prevent cross-contamination while maintaining operator protection. An external water bottle with a self-centering bottle depression design allowing bottle replacement without removing the cage from the rack; bottle cap must be cone-shaped in order to maximize water availability and manufactured from welding-free AISI 316 Stainless Steel. Bottle must have a silicone gasket around the neck and a silicone O-ring on the sipper stem to prevent leaks and provide an easy recapping process. A universal, autoclavable plastic card holder compatible with standard facility cage cards of any size, designed with a shape that also unlocks the filter retainer for microbiological filter replacement. Manufacturer documentation demonstrates successful completion of dimensional, functional, washing, sterilization, and durability validation testing for all major cage components. 4.1.2 Rack Technical Requirements Rack frame constructed

hanges via self-centering bottle access that does not require cage removal from the rack. Reducing maintenance time through tool-free plenum removal and tool-free AHU pre-filter replacement. Reducing energy and consumable operating costs through ECM-driven AHUs (50% less power consumption, 90% less heat loss) and multi-linking of multiple racks to a single AHU. Reducing facility footprint per cage through high-density ERGO/HD rack configurations (up to 80 cages on a single double-sided HD rack). Reducing unplanned downtime and maintenance costs relative to the legacy system through modern, currently supported components and assured OEM parts availability. Improving staff safety and ergonomics, reducing repetitive-motion injury risk and associated lost-time costs relative to the legacy latch-based system. Simplifying sanitation and rack processing and maintaining compatibility with existing cage wash and sterilization workflows. 4.6 Sustainability The system shall support NIH sustainability goals by: Operating with high energy efficiency through ECM motor technology (50% less power consumption, 90% less heat loss than legacy AHU technology).
